questions.q: A 4-year-old child presents with a poorly defined, reddish-blue plaque on the forearm that has remained stable in size over 2 years with overlying hypertrichosis. Histology shows nodules of spindle-shaped endothelial cells confined to the mid-to-deep dermis. According to the ISSVA classification and the Kasabach-Merritt spectrum concept, how should this lesion be categorized?
opts: Locally aggressive borderline vascular tumor requiring immediate systemic chemotherapy
Benign vascular tumor (tufted angioma) representing the superficial, mild end of the KHE spectrum, still carrying risk of Kasabach-Merritt Phenomenon
GLUT1-positive infantile hemangioma with atypical superficial presentation
Congenital hemangioma (RICH subtype) that will undergo spontaneous complete involution
questions.exp: This clinical and histopathological presentation is characteristic of tufted angioma, which ISSVA technically classifies as benign but which exists on the same biological spectrum as kaposiform hemangioendothelioma. Despite its benign classification and superficial indolent behavior, tufted angioma shares the capacity with KHE to trigger Kasabach-Merritt Phenomenon. The dermis-confined location with spindle-shaped endothelial cell nodules and lack of spontaneous involution are key distinguishing features.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 3] Kaposiform Haemangioendothelioma and Tufted Angioma

questions.q: A 24-year-old woman presents with sharply demarcated symmetric erythema and petechiae of the hands and feet with an abrupt demarcation line at the wrists and ankles, accompanied by an enanthem on the lips and soft palate. This clinical presentation most closely matches which parvovirus B19-associated syndrome?
opts: Classic erythema infectiosum with secondary bacterial infection
Papular-purpuric gloves and socks syndrome (PPGSS)
Erythema infectiosum occurring in an immunocompromised adult
Parvovirus B19-induced necrotizing vasculitis
questions.exp: Papular-purpuric gloves and socks syndrome (PPGSS) is a distinct acral variant of parvovirus B19 infection characterized by symmetric edema, erythema, and petechiae of the distal hands and feet with a sharp demarcation line at the wrists and ankles. Unlike classic erythema infectiosum, which predominantly affects school-aged children, PPGSS is most commonly seen in young adults. The enanthem involvement and dermoscopic features are pathognomonic for this variant.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine a YOUNG ADULT wearing RED GLOVES and RED SOCKS with a SHARP CUT-OFF line at the wrists and ankles—like she stopped mid-dressing at the castle entrance; the RED extends only to the GLOVE and SOCK boundaries, nowhere else.

questions.q: A skin biopsy of a blueberry muffin baby reveals poorly circumscribed, plaque-like aggregates of nucleated erythroid precursor cells, immature leukocytes, and megakaryocytes within the dermis. Which layer of the skin is primarily affected by this pathological process?
opts: Stratum corneum and epidermis exclusively
Superficial vascular plexus, reticular dermis, and occasionally subcutaneous fat
Subcutaneous panniculus only
Epidermal-dermal junction with vasculitis
questions.exp: The blueberry muffin sign represents cutaneous extramedullary hematopoiesis centered on the superficial vascular plexus and extending diffusely throughout the reticular dermis and occasionally into subcutaneous fat. The pathology lacks true inflammation or vasculitis, distinguishing it from autoimmune bullous diseases. Notably, the epidermis is spared in this morphological reaction pattern.

questions.q: A term neonate develops a prodrome of fever and irritability followed by faint orange-red macules with flexural accentuation. Within 48 hours, tissue-paper-like wrinkling progresses to widespread exfoliation with large areas of denuded skin resembling a scalded appearance. Gram-positive cocci are cultured from what anatomical site, suggesting the primary source of infection?
opts: Bullae fluid at the site of exfoliation
An occult distant focus such as purulent conjunctivitis or omphalitis
Cerebrospinal fluid
Urine culture
questions.exp: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) differs from localized bullous impetigo in that exfoliative toxins act systemically, diffusing hematogenously from a distant, often occult primary focus of infection such as purulent conjunctivitis, omphalitis, or a colonized umbilical stump. The bullae fluid at the site of exfoliation is characteristically sterile because the toxins act remotely rather than locally, distinguishing SSSS from localized bullous impetigo where organisms are cultured from blister fluid.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine the castle's EYE (conjunctivitis), BELLY BUTTON (omphalitis), or UMBILICAL ROPE hidden as the POISON SOURCE—toxins travel through SECRET UNDERGROUND TUNNELS (bloodstream) to FLOOD the whole castle (SSSS), but the VISIBLE FLOOD WATERS (bullae) are EMPTY of germs because the poison was BREWED ELSEWHERE.

questions.q: A 3-week-old infant presents with widespread, asymptomatic brown macules distributed in a linear streaky pattern following the lines of Blaschko on the trunk and extremities. Histology shows increased melanin within basal keratinocytes with normal melanocyte count and no dermal melanophages. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Hypomelanosis of Ito
Linear and Whorled Nevoid Hypermelanosis (LWNH)
Segmental neurofibromatosis type 1
Incontinentia pigmenti
questions.exp: LWNH presents in the first few weeks of life with diffuse, streaky hyperpigmented macules following Blaschko lines, lacking any preceding inflammatory or vesicular stage. The characteristic histology shows epidermal melanotic hypermelanosis with increased melanin in basal keratinocytes, normal melanocyte numbers, and crucially, no dermal melanophages—distinguishing it from incontinentia pigmenti where pigment incontinence occurs.

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with symmetric, shiny, glazed erythema on the balls of his feet and heel areas that he reports as painful and fissured. On examination, the interdigital web spaces and the arches of the feet are completely spared. Which of the following is the MOST important distinguishing feature that differentiates this condition from tinea pedis?
opts: Presence of superficial desquamation and scaling
Pathognomonic sparing of the interdigital web spaces and non-weight-bearing instep
Symmetric distribution on weight-bearing surfaces
Associated hyperhidrosis and occlusive footwear use
questions.exp: Juvenile plantar dermatosis characteristically spares the interdigital web spaces (toe clefts) and non-weight-bearing instep areas, which is the primary clinical feature that distinguishes it from tinea pedis, where web space involvement is common. While all other features are present in JPD, this specific topographical sparing pattern is pathognomonic.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture the ARCHES of a medieval castle COMPLETELY UNTOUCHED by invaders while the WEIGHT-BEARING STONE WALKWAYS crumble—those EMPTY ARCHES are your clue to JPD, not fungal infection.

questions.q: A 15-year-old girl with moderate inflammatory acne is started on oral doxycycline. Her mother asks why the dermatologist specifically avoided this drug when the patient was younger. What is the primary concern with tetracycline antibiotics in children <8 years?
opts: Irreversible tooth discoloration and enamel hypoplasia
Increased risk of photosensitivity reactions
Hepatotoxicity requiring monthly liver function tests
Gastrointestinal dysmotility and delayed gastric emptying
questions.exp: Doxycycline and other tetracyclines are contraindicated in children <8 years due to binding of the drug to calcium in developing tooth enamel, causing permanent yellow-brown discoloration and hypoplasia. This is a classic pediatric dermatology safety point and frequently appears on board exams. The other side effects are either not specific to this age group or not the primary reason for age restriction.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine an 8-YEAR-OLD CHILD with YELLOW-BROWN VAMPIRE FANGS (tetracycline staining) emerging from the castle dungeon—the calcium-binding monsters attack only before age 8, when teeth are still forming.

questions.q: A 3-week-old presents with shedding of the collodion membrane, revealing large, dark-brown, plate-like scales in a bark-like mosaic pattern, severe ectropion, eclabium, scarring alopecia, and extreme heat intolerance. Which gene mutation most commonly causes this presentation?
opts: *ALOX12B* encoding lipoxygenase
*TGM1* encoding transglutaminase-1
*NIPAL4* encoding ichthyin
*CYP4F22* encoding vitamin A metabolism enzyme
questions.exp: The clinical presentation of large, dark-brown, plate-like scales in a bark-like mosaic pattern with severe ectropion, eclabium, scarring alopecia, and extreme heat intolerance is characteristic of lamellar ichthyosis, which is most commonly caused by inactivating mutations in the *TGM1* gene encoding transglutaminase-1. This enzyme is essential for formation of the cornified cell envelope within the stratum corneum.

questions.q: A 14-year-old boy presents with a well-demarcated, irregularly bordered tan-brown patch on his left shoulder with coarse dark terminal hairs erupting over it. The patch has a bizarre, jagged outline resembling an archipelago. Which genetic mutation is primarily responsible for the pathogenesis of this lesion?
opts: Postzygotic somatic mutations in the ACTB gene affecting pilar smooth muscle cells
Germline BRAF V600E mutation causing constitutive MAPK pathway activation
Loss-of-function mutations in the NF1 gene on chromosome 17
Gain-of-function mutations in the PTEN gene affecting melanocyte proliferation
questions.exp: Becker's nevus is driven by postzygotic somatic mutations in the ACTB gene (encoding beta-actin), which potentiate Hedgehog pathway signaling and disrupt hair follicle and pilar muscle development. Laser microdissection has proven these mutations are primarily located within the pilar smooth muscle cells of the lesional area. The condition follows a paradominant inheritance pattern, occurring almost always sporadically as a mosaic trait.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine ACTB (ACTion Beta-actin) muscular BUILDERS constructing pilar MUSCLES in the castle's shoulder tower—their mutations make HAIRY, PIGMENTED ARCHIPELAGO blueprints.

questions.q: A 5-day-old neonate presents with multiple flaccid bullae (1–2 cm) filled with clear yellow fluid on the perineum and neck folds. The bullae rupture within 24–48 hours leaving thin, shiny golden-yellow crusts with a peripheral collarette of scale. Nikolsky sign is negative and mucous membranes are spared. What is the specific target antigen cleaved by the staphylococcal exfoliative toxins in this condition?
opts: Desmoglein 3 (Dsg3)
Desmoglein 1 (Dsg1)
α3-β1 integrin
Occludin
questions.exp: Bullous impetigo of the newborn is mediated by staphylococcal exfoliative toxins (ETA or ETB) that act as trypsin-like serine proteases and specifically cleave desmoglein 1 (Dsg1), a desmosomal cadherin responsible for cell-to-cell adhesion in the superficial epidermis. This results in subcorneal acantholytic blister formation characteristic of localized bullous impetigo.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture Dsg1 as a golden CHAIN LINK holding the SHALLOW (superficial) castle floor together—when the toxin SCISSORS (serine protease) cut it, the FLOOR COLLAPSES inward at the GRAIN CELLAR (stratum granulosum), spilling treasure (blister fluid) that dries to VARNISH (golden crusts).

questions.q: A 7-year-old with classic molluscum contagiosum develops an eczematous inflammatory halo surrounding several lesions. The parents are concerned this indicates secondary bacterial infection. What does this inflammatory response actually represent?
opts: Secondary bacterial superinfection requiring antibiotic treatment
A robust host immune response involving plasmacytoid dendritic cells and cytotoxic T lymphocytes that often precedes spontaneous viral clearance
Progression to giant molluscum requiring immediate intervention
Meyerson's phenomenon indicating systemic immunodeficiency
questions.exp: The eczematous inflammatory halo around molluscum papules is termed Meyerson's phenomenon and represents a robust host immune response, not a bacterial infection. This inflammation frequently precedes spontaneous resolution and clearance of the virus, indicating favorable immune recognition rather than disease progression.

questions.q: A 6-year-old child presents with a bright red, confluent macular erythema strictly localized to both cheeks with sparing of the nasal bridge and circumoral regions. The mother reports a mild prodrome of low-grade fever and headache 3 days ago. Which statement regarding infectivity at the time of rash appearance is correct?
opts: The patient remains highly infectious via respiratory droplets when the cutaneous rash appears
The patient is no longer infectious once the cutaneous rash appears
The patient becomes infectious only after the lacy reticulated rash develops on the extremities
Infectivity persists throughout the entire clinical course of the disease
questions.exp: Parvovirus B19 (Fifth Disease) follows a characteristic two-stage rash pattern: first the 'slapped cheek' appearance on the face, then lacy reticulated eruption on extremities. Crucially, patients are no longer infectious once the cutaneous rash appears, making early diagnosis important for infection control in schools. The viral replication peaks during the prodromal phase before rash onset.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a SLAPPED CHEEK so RED it's LOCKED BEHIND CASTLE GATES—once you SEE the red cheek (rash), the gates CLOSE and the virus ESCAPES; the contagious GHOST already LEFT when the rash ARRIVED.

questions.q: A 2-year-old boy presents with multiple reddish-brown macules and papules on his trunk and thighs. Stroking one lesion produces immediate localized whealing and erythema. Genetic testing reveals a KIT D816V mutation. Which layer of the dermis is primarily affected in this patient's condition?
opts: Reticular dermis with deep subcutaneous extension
Papillary dermis around superficial blood vessels and adnexae
Mid-dermis at the dermal-hypodermal junction
Subcutaneous fat with sparse dermal involvement
questions.exp: Maculopapular cutaneous mastocytosis (urticaria pigmentosa) is characterized by mast cell infiltration primarily in the papillary dermis, with cells accumulating around superficial blood vessels and adnexal structures. The positive Darier's sign reflects rapid mast cell degranulation in this superficial layer when mechanically stimulated.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture PAPILLARY DERMIS as the SHALLOW MOAT surrounding the castle's SUPERFICIAL towers (blood vessels), where mast cell guards stand ready to WHEEZE and ERECT immediately when you STROKE the drawbridge—UP from UP (Urticaria Pigmentosa).

questions.q: Which enterovirus is responsible for severe hand-foot-and-mouth disease with a documented propensity for brainstem encephalitis and acute flaccid paralysis, and has been the cause of recurrent massive epidemics in the Asia-Pacific region since the late 1990s?
opts: Coxsackievirus A16
Coxsackievirus A6
Enterovirus 71
Echovirus type 5
questions.exp: Enterovirus 71 (EV-A71) causes the severe neurologic variant of HFMD with CNS and cardiopulmonary tropism, leading to brainstem encephalitis, encephalomyelitis, aseptic meningitis, and acute flaccid paralysis. This virus has been responsible for large, severe epidemics throughout the Asia-Pacific region (Taiwan, China, Singapore, Malaysia, Vietnam, Australia) since the late 1990s, with highest mortality in children under 5 years.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: EV71 is the EVIL SEVEN-ONE virus—imagine it storming through ASIA-PACIFIC castles wearing a BRAINSTEM crown, causing FLACCID knights to collapse in PARALYSIS, while EPIDEMIC flags wave across Taiwan, China, and Singapore.

questions.q: A 6-year-old boy presents with multiple dome-shaped, pearly-white papules with central umbilication on his trunk and arms. Genotypic analysis is performed. Which MCV subtype is most likely responsible for this presentation?
opts: MCV-2
MCV-1
MCV-3
MCV-4
questions.exp: MCV-1 is the most dominant subtype worldwide and is responsible for 76–98% of childhood molluscum contagiosum infections, particularly in the United States. MCV-2 is predominantly sexually transmitted in adults and is prevalent in immunosuppressed individuals. MCV-3 and MCV-4 are extremely rare.

questions.q: Pigmentary mosaicism in a newborn results from a somatic postzygotic mutation occurring during early embryogenesis. Which of the following is the PRIMARY reason these lesions follow predictable distribution patterns such as the lines of Blaschko or leaf-like (phylloid) patterns?
opts: Autoimmune targeting of melanocytes along developmental seams
Directional proliferation and outward migration of embryonic keratinocytes and melanoblasts during neural crest migration
Age-related progressive dermal infiltration by inflammatory cells
HLA-associated immune receptor activation in genetically predisposed individuals
questions.exp: Pigmentary mosaicism patterns reflect the embryonic migration pathways of mutated cell clones—Blaschko lines represent keratinocyte migration from the neural crest, while phylloid patterns represent the migration of single melanoblasts. These are purely developmental/structural anomalies arising from somatic mutations, completely devoid of autoimmune, inflammatory, or HLA-associated mechanisms.

questions.q: A 2-day-old neonate presents with a generalized eruption of discrete, dark blue, non-blanching macules and papules (2–10 mm) across the trunk and extremities. The mother reports a febrile illness with rash during the first trimester of pregnancy. Which of the following intracerebral imaging findings would be most characteristic of the likely causative pathogen?
opts: Periventricular calcifications only
Diffuse/tram-track calcifications
Multiple cortical microabscesses
Subdural hemorrhage
questions.exp: The first-trimester maternal infection with rash strongly suggests congenital toxoplasmosis, which presents with characteristic diffuse or tram-track intracerebral calcifications. Periventricular calcifications are the hallmark of CMV. The blueberry muffin sign in this clinical context results from cutaneous extramedullary hematopoiesis driven by overwhelming fetal parasitemia.

questions.q: A 13-year-old boy with Becker's nevus on his upper trunk is noted to have a male-to-female sex predilection ratio of 5:1 in the isolated form. Which hormonal receptor is uniquely and strongly linked to driving the clinical evolution and progression of this lesion?
opts: Androgen receptor with heightened localized sensitivity and increased receptor density in lesional skin
Estrogen receptor alpha mediating systemic hyperpigmentation
Melanocyte-stimulating hormone receptor promoting melanin synthesis
Thyroid hormone receptor triggering dermal fibroblast proliferation
questions.exp: Becker's nevus progression is directly driven by localized heightened sensitivity to circulating androgens, accompanied by a documented increase in the density and activity of androgen receptors within lesional skin. This androgen-driven pathogenesis explains the dramatic growth and hypertrichosis during adolescence/puberty and accounts for the striking male predominance in the classic isolated form.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: ANDROGENS (masculine WARRIOR KINGS) sit on THRONE RECEPTORS in the upper TRUNK CASTLE, triggering PUBERTY'S hair EXPLOSION and pigment ARMY during adolescence.

questions.q: A 4-year-old boy presents with painful vesicles on his palms and soles following oral ulcers on the buccal mucosa and hard palate. The vesicles are described as elliptical with their long axes running parallel to skin lines. Skin biopsy shows intraepidermal vesicles with vacuolar degeneration of keratinocytes, but notably absent are viral inclusion bodies and multinucleated giant cells. Which virus is the most likely causative agent?
opts: Enterovirus 71
Coxsackievirus A16
Herpes simplex virus type 1
Varicella-zoster virus
questions.exp: Classic hand-foot-and-mouth disease is most commonly caused by Coxsackievirus A16 (CVA16). The characteristic elliptical 'football-shaped' vesicles with axes parallel to dermatoglyphics, combined with the absence of viral inclusion bodies and multinucleated giant cells on histology, distinguish HFMD from HSV and varicella, which would show these cytopathic features. Enterovirus 71 causes the severe neurologic variant.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: A 16-year-old BOY (CVA16) plays FOOTBALL at the PALM tree SPA during SUMMER, drawing PARALLEL lines with his finger on the sand—no GIANT HEADS in the game, just classic fun.

questions.q: A 6-year-old boy with a history of atopy presents with bilateral shiny, fissured lesions on the forefoot and toe pads that developed after a summer spent in a swimming pool and wearing synthetic sneakers. Histopathology, if performed, would most likely show the characteristic pathological finding of inflammation localized to which anatomical structure?
opts: Sebaceous glands and hair follicles
Acrosyringium and eccrine sweat ducts
Dermal collagen bundles and elastic fibers
Blood vessels and lymphatic channels
questions.exp: The hallmark histological finding in juvenile plantar dermatosis, despite the condition being primarily diagnosed clinically, is inflammation specifically targeting the acrosyringium and eccrine sweat ducts. This reflects the underlying mechanism of barrier disruption from repeated maceration and drying cycles in an occlusive, humid environment.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: In the castle's SWEAT LODGE (acrosyringium), tiny DUCTS are under SIEGE—the SWEATY SOCK scenario creates inflammation RIGHT AT THE SWEAT GLAND OPENING where wet meets dry.

questions.q: A 3-month-old infant presents with a deep, infiltrative vascular lesion on the neck that crosses tissue planes into the subcutis. On laboratory testing, the child has thrombocytopenia and prolonged PT/INR. Which of the following best explains the relationship between this tumor type and the laboratory findings?
opts: The tumor is GLUT1-positive infantile hemangioma, which triggers consumptive coagulopathy through platelet sequestration
The tumor is kaposiform hemangioendothelioma, which shares a unique capacity with tufted angioma to trigger Kasabach-Merritt Phenomenon through inappropriate endothelial proliferation
The tumor is pyogenic granuloma with secondary infection leading to disseminated intravascular coagulation
The tumor is congenital hemangioma that spontaneously involutes, causing transient coagulopathy during regression
questions.exp: Kaposiform hemangioendothelioma (KHE) and tufted angioma represent a biological spectrum unified by their shared, unique capacity to trigger Kasabach-Merritt Phenomenon (KMP)—a life-threatening consumptive coagulopathy. This distinguishes them sharply from GLUT1-positive infantile hemangioma, which never causes KMP. The inappropriately proliferating blood and lymphatic endothelial cells in these tumors are responsible for the coagulopathy.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 3] Kaposiform Haemangioendothelioma and Tufted Angioma

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with depigmented patches on his left arm and chest that appeared 6 months ago. The lesions are unilateral, band-shaped, and stopped abruptly at the midline. Which of the following best describes the pathological target and primary immune mechanism in this clinical presentation?
opts: Structural melanin defect in the stratum corneum; primary role of neutrophilic infiltration
Mature melanocytes in the basal layer and hair follicle bulge; CD8+ cytotoxic T cells driven by IFN-γ and CXCL10 signaling
Melanocyte precursor cells in the dermis; primary role of humoral antibody responses
Tyrosinase enzyme deficiency inherited as an autosomal recessive trait; no inflammatory component
questions.exp: Vitiligo is an acquired, cell-mediated autoimmune disease targeting mature, functional melanocytes in the basal epidermis and hair follicle bulge. The pathogenic cascade is driven by autoreactive CD8+ cytotoxic T cells recognizing melanocyte autoantigens (tyrosinase, TYRP1, DCT, MCHR1, SOX10), with the IFN-γ and CXCL10 chemokine axis playing a central role. Segmental vitiligo, as described here, accounts for 15–30% of pediatric cases and follows quasi-dermatomal or Blaschkoid patterns.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a SEGMENTED KNIGHT (segmental vitiligo) guarding the BASAL LAYER CASTLE WALL, with CD8+ CYTOTOXIC ASSASSINS (T cells) firing GAMMA-RAY ARROWS (IFN-γ) and CXCL10 GRAPPLING HOOKS across the midline—stopping abruptly at the castle moat.

questions.q: A 4-month-old infant with severe atopic dermatitis unresponsive to topical therapies is referred for biologic therapy. Which of the following biologics is FDA-approved for use at this age?
opts: Dupilumab (IL-4Rα inhibitor)
Tralokinumab (IL-13 inhibitor)
Abrocitinib (JAK1 inhibitor)
Ruxolitinib cream (JAK inhibitor)
questions.exp: Dupilumab is the only biologic approved for atopic dermatitis in infants as young as 6 months. Tralokinumab is approved only for adults (≥18 yrs), while abrocitinib and ruxolitinib require age ≥12 years. Dupilumab targets IL-4 receptor alpha and was the first biologic approved in such a young pediatric population.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a 6-MONTH-OLD BABY riding a DUPLICATE (Dupilumab) horse through the castle—the ONLY steed young enough for the nursery wing, while all other biologics are locked in the adult tower (18+ years).

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with a rapidly growing, dome-shaped, firm papule on his neck that is 5 mm in diameter with a reddish-pink color. Histology reveals large epithelioid and spindle-shaped melanocytes with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, prominent nucleoli, and characteristic dull-pink acellular globules at the dermal-epidermal junction. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Classic Spitz nevus
Pigmented spindle cell nevus (Reed nevus)
Common acquired nevus
Melanoma
questions.exp: The clinical presentation of a rapidly growing dome-shaped papule in a child <10 years, combined with the pathognomonic histological finding of Kamino bodies (dull-pink, acellular, PAS-positive basement membrane material at the DEJ) and maturation with depth, is diagnostic of classic Spitz nevus. The epidermis overlying Spitz nevi is thin and fragile, explaining the risk of bleeding with minor trauma.

questions.q: A 2-day-old neonate presents with a 3.5 cm tan-to-brown patch on the left thigh with coarse terminal hair. Which genetic mutation is most likely responsible for this lesion, and what is its detection frequency in congenital melanocytic nevi?
opts: BRAF V600E mutation, detected in ~70–80% of cases
NRAS mutation at codon 61, detected in ~70–80% of cases
TP53 mutation, detected in ~50% of cases
KIT mutation, detected in ~60% of cases
questions.exp: NRAS mutations at codon 61 are the most prevalent genetic driver of congenital melanocytic nevi, found in approximately 70–80% of cases. These mutations occur via postzygotic somatic events in the MAPK signaling cascade and are strongly associated with larger lesions, satellite nevi, and neurological involvement. BRAF mutations are occasionally present but are less common and more typical of smaller CMNs.

questions.q: What is the primary genetic driver of approximately 55% of Spitz nevi, and how does this differ from common acquired nevi and melanomas?
opts: BRAF mutations; same as common acquired nevi
Kinase fusions involving ALK, ROS1, NTRK1, NTRK3, BRAF, RET, and MET; different from the BRAF/NRAS mutations typical of common nevi and melanomas
NRAS mutations with chromosome 11p copy number increase; identical to melanoma pathogenesis
TP53 mutations; unique to pediatric melanocytic lesions
questions.exp: Approximately 55% of Spitz nevi are driven by mutually exclusive kinase fusions (ALK, ROS1, NTRK1, NTRK3, BRAF, RET, MET), which distinguishes them genetically from common acquired nevi and melanomas that are typically driven by BRAF or NRAS point mutations. An additional 15% of Spitz nevi harbour HRAS mutations often with isolated chromosome 11p copy number increase.

questions.q: A 10-year-old girl with a family history of Hashimoto's thyroiditis and alopecia areata develops symmetric depigmented macules on her face, neck, and extremities over 8 months. Histopathology of an early lesion shows a sparse band-like superficial infiltrate at the dermoepidermal junction with complete absence of melanocytes on Melan-A immunostaining. Which genetic/HLA feature most directly explains the co-occurrence of her vitiligo with her family's autoimmune thyroid disease?
opts: Vitiligo and Hashimoto's thyroiditis share identical HLA-B27 alleles, which encode cross-reactive T-cell epitopes
Both conditions result from loss-of-function mutations in the FOXP3 gene affecting regulatory T cells

Vitiligo and Hashimoto's disease share a polygenic autoimmune background; GWAS has identified ~50 susceptibility loci encoding immune-regulating proteins (HLA, PTPN22, NALP1, IFIH1) common to both conditions
Thyroid peroxidase antibodies directly cross-react with tyrosinase on melanocytes, causing simultaneous autoimmune damage
questions.exp: Vitiligo is a polygenic disorder, and genome-wide association studies have identified approximately 50 susceptibility loci, the vast majority of which encode immune-regulating proteins (HLA genes, PTPN22, NALP1, IFIH1). Vitiligo shares this genetic autoimmune background with other endocrinopathies, resulting in strong clinical associations with autoimmune thyroid disease (Hashimoto's), Type 1 diabetes, Addison's disease, and alopecia areata. The shared genetic susceptibility rather than direct antigen cross-reactivity explains the familial clustering of autoimmune conditions.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: In the GENETIC LIBRARY of the castle, imagine 50 GOLDEN IMMUNE-REGULATING KEYS (GWAS loci: HLA, PTPN22, NALP1, IFIH1) hanging on the same wall, unlocking BOTH the THYROID VAULT and the MELANOCYTE CHAMBER—shared keys for shared autoimmune troubles.

questions.q: A 6-month-old infant is evaluated for multiple congenital melanocytic nevi (n=15) ranging from 2–8 cm each across the trunk and extremities. The parents inquire about the risk of serious neurological complications. What is the primary neurological syndrome associated with this presentation?
opts: Sturge–Weber syndrome with facial port-wine stains and seizures
Neurocutaneous melanosis, associated with melanosis of the leptomeninges and CNS melanoma
Neurofibromatosis type 1 with café-au-lait macules and optic nerve gliomas
Tuberous sclerosis with cortical hamartomas and cardiac rhabdomyomas
questions.exp: Neurocutaneous melanosis is the primary neurological complication associated with multiple medium-to-large congenital melanocytic nevi, particularly when three or more medium CMNs are present. This syndrome involves aberrant melanocytic infiltration of the leptomeninges and brain parenchyma, conferring risk for primary CNS melanoma and neurological sequelae. The presence of multiple satellite nevi substantially elevates this risk even without a giant nevus.

questions.q: A 2-week-old neonate born at 36 weeks presents with a taut, shiny, transparent parchment-like membrane covering the entire body. Which histological finding is the primary hallmark of the collodion membrane?
opts: Markedly thickened, compact, orthokeratotic stratum corneum with normal underlying epidermis and dermis
Spongiosis and intercellular edema throughout the epidermis
Dilated dermal blood vessels with perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate
Dyskeratosis and acantholysis in the suprabasal layers
questions.exp: The collodion baby phenotype is characterized histologically by a markedly thickened, compact, orthokeratotic stratum corneum, while the underlying epidermis and dermis remain relatively normal. This distinctive finding is consistent across all genetic subtypes of congenital disorders of cornification that present with collodion baby phenotype.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man has systemic mastocytosis confirmed by bone marrow biopsy. Flow cytometry reveals aberrant mast cells co-expressing CD117, CD25, and CD2. Which of the following best explains why these immunophenotypic markers distinguish clonal mastocytosis mast cells from reactive mast cells?
opts: CD25 and CD2 are markers of autoimmune activation against mast cell autoantigens
Normal reactive mast cells lack CD25 and CD2 expression; only clonal neoplastic mast cells aberrantly co-express these markers
CD25 and CD2 indicate HLA-associated mast cell infiltration typical of allergic responses
These markers identify pathogenic autoantibodies bound to mast cell surface receptors
questions.exp: Mastocytosis is a clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm driven by KIT mutations, not autoimmunity. The aberrant mast cells uniquely express CD25 and CD2 as part of their neoplastic phenotype, whereas normal reactive mast cells strictly lack these markers. This immunophenotypic distinction is critical for flow cytometric diagnosis of systemic mastocytosis.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: In the castle armory, CLONAL CLONE soldiers wear DUAL BADGES (CD25 + CD2) sewn onto their armor—normal REACTIVE guards have NO badges. The mutant KIT (CD117) KEY opens doors only ABERRANT clones can unlock, never autoimmune peasants storming the gates.
